blocks.recap_md: Every powerful language has three mechanisms: primitive expressions, means of combination, and means of abstraction; this chapter focuses on building procedures over simple numerical data.
The Scheme interpreter evaluates primitive number expressions; a combination applies an operator to the values of its operands.
A combination consists of an operator and operands; prefix notation places the operator first, naturally supporting an arbitrary number of operands.
Prefix notation's second advantage is that it extends straightforwardly to nested combinations of arbitrary complexity.
Pretty-printing makes the structure of deeply nested expressions clear; the interpreter runs a read-eval-print loop, evaluating and printing automatically.

knowledge_items.statement: When evaluating a combination, the interpreter first recursively evaluates the operator and each operand, then applies the resulting procedure to the argument values.
Prefix notation places the operator to the left of the operands, so it naturally accommodates an arbitrary number of arguments and allows unambiguous nesting.
The Scheme interpreter runs a read-eval-print loop: it reads an expression, evaluates it, and automatically prints the result - the user never has to explicitly ask for the value to be printed.

questions.prompt: When evaluating the combination (+ (* 2 3) 4), what is the actual order of evaluation the interpreter follows?
options: It recursively evaluates the operator and each operand (here, (* 2 3) and 4), then applies the resulting procedure to those values
It scans the expression character by character from left to right and prints it directly, without recursive evaluation
It performs a string-substitution expansion of the whole expression first, then evaluates it all at once
It only evaluates the outermost operator; operands are passed in unevaluated, and the operator decides internally when to evaluate them
questions.explanation: SICP emphasizes that evaluating a combination follows the rule of evaluate-then-apply: recursively evaluate each subexpression (the operator and each operand), then apply the resulting procedure to the argument values.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of prefix notation (like (+ 1 2 3)) over infix notation (like 1 + 2 + 3)?
options: The operator is always leftmost, so it naturally supports an arbitrary number of operands and combinations can nest without ambiguity
Prefix notation evaluates faster than infix notation
Prefix notation lets you omit parentheses, making expressions shorter
Prefix notation is just a Lisp-specific syntactic convention with no effect on expressive power, purely historical habit
questions.explanation: The text explicitly names two advantages of prefix notation: it accommodates an arbitrary number of arguments, and it nests without ambiguity - neither is about evaluation speed or parenthesis count.

questions.prompt: In the Scheme interpreter's read-eval-print loop, does the user need to explicitly tell the interpreter to print the value of an expression?
options: No - the read-eval-print loop itself automatically prints the result after every evaluation
Yes, an explicit call to something like a print procedure is required to see the result
Only in an interactive terminal; running as a script wouldn't print automatically
Only when the return value is a number; other types need to be printed manually
questions.explanation: The text specifically notes that it is not necessary to explicitly instruct the interpreter to print the value of an expression - that's exactly what the read-eval-print loop does, over and over.
